Started, I want to say nineteen. In production, two. And one of those two is a chatbot on our internal help desk that I would describe as barely alive.

What's the most common reason one stalls?

[]
Sam Forrester 4:54
There's no owner on the other side. Data science builds it, and then it needs to live somewhere, and the platform team's roadmap is full, and there's no budget line for running it. So it just sits in a repo.

[]
Tim Olutayo 5:41
For us it's the last mile. The model is fine. Getting it in front of a nurse, inside the software the nurse already uses, requires an integration nobody scoped and a vendor who doesn't want to do it.

Who decides a pilot is finished?

[]
Nadia Kohl 7:15
Nobody. That's the actual answer. Closing it means writing down that it didn't work, and the person who sponsored it is now a VP.

[]
Sam Forrester 8:02
We have a project that has been ninety percent done for fourteen months. Every status report says ninety percent.

[]
Priya Raghunathan 8:49
What does that cost you, given nobody cancelled it?

[]
Tim Olutayo 9:36
We added it up last quarter because Finance asked. Cloud spend on idle endpoints for the stalled projects was about eleven thousand a month. That's not the real cost though. The real cost is that we can't get approval for a new one, because the last six are still open.

[]
Nadia Kohl 10:23
That's exactly it. The graveyard is what's blocking the next thing.
